title: 2 Kings 19:20–37
context: Isaiah sends word that the LORD has heard Hezekiah’s prayer, and he delivers a poem in which Zion scorns the arrogant king of Assyria, who has defied the Holy One of Israel and does not realize that the LORD planned long ago what Assyria has done. The LORD promises a sign of three years of recovering harvests, a remnant that will take root and bear fruit, and that the king of Assyria will not come into the city or shoot an arrow there, because the LORD will defend it for his own sake and for David’s sake. That night the LORD’s angel strikes one hundred eighty-five thousand in the Assyrian camp, Sennacherib returns to Nineveh, and later, while worshiping Nisroch, he is struck down by Adrammelech and Sharezer, though the text does not say how long afterward. The account appears also in Isaiah 37:21–38 and in briefer form in 2 Chronicles 32:21. Arminian and Reformed readers commonly treat the passage as shared ground about the LORD answering prayer, humbling pride, and keeping his promise to David.

verses.text: Then Isaiah the son of Amoz sent to Hezekiah, saying, “The LORD, the God of Israel, says ‘You have prayed to me against Sennacherib king of Assyria, and I have heard you.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Isaiah sending word that the LORD has heard Hezekiah’s prayer against Sennacherib. Prayer is genuinely answered.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD’s answer as the means by which he brings his purpose to pass. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as assurance that God hears his people.

verses.text: This is the word that the LORD has spoken concerning him: ‘The virgin daughter of Zion has despised you and ridiculed you. The daughter of Jerusalem has shaken her head at you.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the virgin daughter of Zion despising and mocking the Assyrian king. The besieged city is pictured as unafraid.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the image as God’s perspective on the enemy, who is not to be feared (compare Psalm 2:4). Both traditions commonly read the verse as a reversal of the taunts in chapter 18.

verses.text: Whom have you defied and blasphemed? Against whom have you exalted your voice and lifted up your eyes on high? Against the Holy One of Israel!
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD asking whom the Assyrian king has defied and blasphemed. The answer is the Holy One of Israel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as revealing that the conflict is ultimately with God himself. Readers in both traditions commonly read it as the turning point of the poem.

verses.text: By your messengers, you have defied the Lord, and have said, “With the multitude of my chariots, I have come up to the height of the mountains, to the innermost parts of Lebanon, and I will cut down its tall cedars and its choice cypress trees; and I will enter into his farthest lodging place, the forest of his fruitful field.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Assyrian king boasting of his chariots, his conquests, and cutting down the cedars of Lebanon. His pride is vast.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the boast as human arrogance claiming what belongs to God. Both traditions commonly read the verse as a portrait of self-exalting power.

verses.text: I have dug and drunk strange waters, and I will dry up all the rivers of Egypt with the sole of my feet.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the king boasting of digging wells and drying up Egypt’s rivers. He imagines himself utterly unstoppable.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the exaggerated claims as pride that will soon be humbled. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as part of the case the LORD answers.

verses.text: Haven’t you heard how I have done it long ago, and formed it of ancient times? Now I have brought it to pass, that it should be yours to lay waste fortified cities into ruinous heaps.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD declaring that he planned long ago what Assyria has done. Even the conqueror’s success lies within God’s purpose.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as a clear statement of God’s sovereign ordering of history (compare Psalm 33:11). Both traditions commonly affirm that Assyria remains responsible for its pride (compare Isaiah 10:12).

verses.text: Therefore their inhabitants had little power. They were dismayed and confounded. They were like the grass of the field and like the green herb, like the grass on the housetops and like grain blasted before it has grown up.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the conquered peoples described as weak, like grass and grain blasted before it grows. Human strength fades quickly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the imagery as showing the frailty of all flesh before God (compare Isaiah 40:6). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a reminder of human transience.

verses.text: But I know your sitting down, your going out, your coming in, and your raging against me.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD saying that he knows the king’s every movement and his raging. Nothing is hidden from God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as affirming God’s complete knowledge of every person (compare Psalm 139:2). Both traditions commonly read it as comfort for God’s people and warning for the proud.

verses.text: Because of your raging against me, and because your arrogance has come up into my ears, therefore I will put my hook in your nose, and my bridle in your lips, and I will turn you back by the way by which you came.’
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD promising to put a hook in the king’s nose and turn him back. The proud conqueror will be led away like an animal.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the image as God’s sovereign restraint of the enemy. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as judgment on arrogance.

verses.text: “This will be the sign to you: This year, you will eat that which grows of itself, and in the second year that which springs from that; and in the third year sow and reap, and plant vineyards and eat their fruit.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the sign of eating what grows of itself for two years and then sowing and reaping. Ordinary life will return.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the sign as God’s pledge of restoration after devastation. Both traditions commonly read the verse as a concrete assurance of God’s care.

verses.text: The remnant that has escaped of the house of Judah will again take root downward, and bear fruit upward.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the escaped remnant of Judah taking root downward and bearing fruit upward. Survival leads to renewed growth.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the remnant as preserved by God for his purposes. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as hope for the future of God’s people.

verses.text: For out of Jerusalem a remnant will go out, and out of Mount Zion those who shall escape. The LORD’s zeal will perform this.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see a remnant going out from Jerusalem, accomplished by the LORD’s zeal. God’s passion secures the future.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD’s zeal as the decisive cause of the remnant’s preservation. Both traditions commonly read the verse as grounding hope in God’s commitment rather than human strength.

verses.text: “Therefore the LORD says concerning the king of Assyria, ‘He will not come to this city, nor shoot an arrow there. He will not come before it with shield, nor cast up a mound against it.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD promising that the Assyrian king will not enter the city, shoot an arrow, or build a siege mound. The deliverance will be complete.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the precise promise as demonstrating God’s control over the outcome. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a word fulfilled in the following verses.

verses.text: He will return the same way that he came, and he will not come to this city,’ says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the king returning the way he came without entering the city. God sets the limits of the enemy’s advance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the repetition as emphasizing the certainty of the LORD’s word. Both traditions commonly read the verse as a solemn assurance.

verses.text: ‘For I will defend this city to save it, for my own sake and for my servant David’s sake.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD defending the city for his own sake and for David’s sake. God’s faithfulness to his promise protects Jerusalem.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as rooted in God’s covenant with David (compare 2 Samuel 7:16; 1 Kings 11:13). Readers in both traditions commonly read it as deliverance grounded in God’s own name and promise.

verses.text: That night, the LORD’s angel went out and struck one hundred eighty-five thousand in the camp of the Assyrians. When men arose early in the morning, behold, these were all dead bodies.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD’s angel striking one hundred eighty-five thousand in the Assyrian camp that night. God acts decisively as he promised.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the event as the LORD’s direct judgment and deliverance (compare Exodus 14:14). Both traditions commonly read the verse as the text presents it, without speculating about how it happened.

verses.text: So Sennacherib king of Assyria departed, went home, and lived at Nineveh.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Sennacherib departing and living at Nineveh. The proud conqueror retreats exactly as the LORD said he would.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the retreat as fulfilling the promise that he would return the way he came. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as the vindication of Isaiah’s word.

verses.text: As he was worshiping in the house of Nisroch his god, Adrammelech and Sharezer struck him with the sword; and they escaped into the land of Ararat. Esar Haddon his son reigned in his place.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Sennacherib struck down by Adrammelech and Sharezer while worshiping in the house of Nisroch his god. The one who mocked the LORD falls before his own idol.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the death as fulfilling the word that he would fall by the sword in his own land (19:7). Both traditions commonly note that the text does not say how much time passed before this happened.
